power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "ps ≥ 0.06", Sentence = "The diagnosed and undiagnosed groups performed similarly on all assessments (ps ≥ 0.06)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: Neural tracking of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal during naturalistic listening in elementary-aged children with and without dyslexia

text.text: Purpose: Children with dyslexia show persistent phonological difficulties in controlled experiments yet often comprehend everyday spoken language successfully.

The present study examined how children with and without dyslexia neurally track phonological, lexical, and syntactic information during naturalistic story listening, and how this tracking relates to reading proficiency.
Study 1 examined neural tracking in 140 typically developing (TD) children.
Study 2 compared children with dyslexia with age-and gender-matched TD controls (n = 35 per group).
Large language model-derived surprisal estimates indexed tracking at each level at exploratory and multiple comparison corrected thresholds.

Results: In TD children, each level of surprisal tracking showed a distinct cortical profile, and higher reading comprehension was associated with greater phonological and syntactic tracking, but reduced lexical tracking.
Children with dyslexia also showed distinct tracking profiles across levels.
In this group, however, higher reading proficiency was associated with greater lexical and syntactic tracking and reduced phonological tracking.
Group contrasts mirrored these patterns.
Children with and without dyslexia differ in how neural tracking of linguistic information relates to reading.
In dyslexia, reduced phonological tracking alongside greater lexical tracking may reflect increased reliance on higher-level linguistic information.
Syntactic tracking was positively related to reading proficiency in both groups, consistent with the protracted development of syntax and its contribution to literacy.
These findings offer new insights into the real-time neurobiology of naturalistic language comprehension and how the interaction of underlying skills may vary in children with dyslexia.
Dyslexia presents a scientific conundrum.
Children with dyslexia struggle with reading while appearing similar to their peers in everyday conversation.

Both awareness of and early screening for dyslexia have increased over the past decades, yet the disorder often remains difficult to detect until reading demands increase in the early elementary grades (Colenbrander et al., 2018).

Our study therefore aims to uncover how children's developing brains track different levels of linguistic information during story listening, and whether children with dyslexia differ from typically developing readers in this tracking.
Reading comprehension, or the ability to derive meaning from written language, builds upon word reading and language comprehension skills (Gough & Tunmer, 1986; Kim, 2020; Tong & Deacon, 2025).

text.text: Language comprehension is a complex ability that draws on multiple levels of linguistic information, including phonological, syntactic, and semantic information at a foundational level (Kim, 2020; Tong & Deacon, 2025).

text.text: Characterizing how these different sources of information contribute to comprehension, including naturalistic narrative listening, has long posed both theoretical and methodological challenges.

Surprisal Theory (Hale, 2001; Levy, 2008) offers one approach to this challenge by characterizing processing load in terms of the contextual predictability of linguistic input: the surprisal of a linguistic unit reflects how unexpected it is given the preceding context.

text.text: Combined with neuroimaging, this framework makes it possible to examine how the brain tracks variation in linguistic surprisal during active comprehension (e.g., Brennan & Hale, 2019; Shain et al., 2024; Willems et al., 2015) and, more recently, how individual differences in this neural tracking relate to children's language and reading abilities, including in children with dyslexia (Klimovich-Gray et al., 2023; Salig et al., preprint).

text.text: This study builds on theoretical and methodological advancements, using child-friendly fNIRS neuroimaging to examine oral comprehension in real time at multiple levels of language processing in typically developing readers (Study 1) and children with dyslexia (Study 2).
Language development emerges through interactions among multiple interacting but partially distinct linguistic systems.
Phonological development provides an early foundation for identifying and organizing the sounds of language (Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Phonological development provides an early foundation for identifying and organizing the sounds of language <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In turn, word learning and gains in lexico-semantic knowledge fine-tune phonological representations, illustrating the reciprocal nature of development across linguistic levels (Werker, 2018).

text.text: Similar interactions characterize the development of syntax and semantics.

Children can use sentence structure to constrain the meanings of unfamiliar words through syntactic bootstrapping (Gleitman, 1990), while familiar words and their meanings can provide a semantic foundation for discovering syntactic regularities (Babineau et al., 2021).

text.text: These interactions continue across childhood as lexical knowledge expands and children comprehend and produce increasingly complex sentence structures (Owens et al., 2024).

text.text: Thus, although phonological, semantic, and syntactic processes are distinguishable language sub-processes, their development is deeply interconnected (Kim, 2020).

text.text: The interconnected nature of language development and processing raises an important question about how potential differences in one language sub-system, such as weaknesses in phonological processes that often characterize dyslexia, might influence the development and functioning of others (Wolf et al., 2024).

text.text: Learning to read provides a particularly important context in which to examine these interactions.
Phonological processing helps children connect language sounds to orthographic representations, a skill especially critical for learning to read in alphabetic languages.
In turn, phonological difficulties typically underlie word-reading difficulties in dyslexia (Wolf et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In turn, phonological difficulties typically underlie word-reading difficulties in dyslexia <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Wolf et al., 2024</ref>).

text.text: Yet, as reflected in the IDA's recent updates to the definition of dyslexia, researchers are finding that language differences associated with dyslexia may extend beyond phonology, while the nature of these differences remain unresolved (IDA, 2025).

For instance, children with dyslexia have shown differences in syntactic processing, yet these differences might be tied to phonological processing rather than reflecting an independent syntactic impairment (Robertson et al., 2024; Rothou & Nisiotis, 2025).

text.text: Children with dyslexia may also experience difficulty with more abstract derivational morphology while drawing on the semantic transparency of free base morphemes as a source of support during word recognition (Eggleston et al., 2024).

text.text: These findings suggest that the critical question may not be whether dyslexia is associated with deficits in each linguistic domain independently, but rather how phonological, semantic, and syntactic information are recruited and integrated during comprehension.
A critical caveat is that studies often use different tasks to measure different language sub-processes (e.g., phonological awareness vs. sentence judgment tasks).

Examining these processes simultaneously during naturalistic spoken-language comprehension may therefore offer a powerful and unique lens for revealing differences that are difficult to capture with standard measures that assess phonological, semantic, and syntactic proficiency separately.

The neural organization supporting language comprehension undergoes increased finetuning to support advanced language processes required for complex language reading comprehension, from relatively broad, temporal-lobe-centered organization toward increasingly specialized frontotemporal networks (Friederici, 2025).

text.text: Building on this framework, the present study uses large language model-derived estimates of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal during naturalistic story listening to offer insights into how the developing brain tracks linguistic information and whether neural response at each level varies by children's reading abilities.

The present study examines how children's brains support language comprehension during naturalistic story listening by characterizing neural sensitivity to phonological, lexical and syntactic predictability.

Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), we modeled hemodynamic responses to large language model-derived estimates of surprisal at these three levels of processing in children ages 7 to 12 (Grades 1 to 5).

This approach allows three levels of linguistic information to be examined simultaneously within a single continuous listening task, rather than across separate tasks designed to isolate different levels of language processing.
Study 1 examined neurobiology of language comprehension in 140 English-speaking typically developing children with no identified language or reading difficulties.

We asked (a) whether and where neural responses track phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal within the language network and (b) how sensitivity to these different levels relates to variation in reading proficiency.
Given the limited developmental fNIRS work using this approach, all analyses within the present study were considered exploratory.

Drawing on prior naturalistic neuroimaging findings with adults (Lopopolo et al., 2017; Heilbron et al., 2022), we expected the three linguistic levels to show partially dissociable patterns of neural tracking.

Study 2 examined neurobiology of language comprehension in children with dyslexia as compared to age-and gender-matched typically developing readers.

We asked (a) whether neural sensitivity to phonological, lexical, and syntactic predictability differs between children with and without dyslexia and (b) how these neural responses relate to reading proficiency across children.

Based on prior research with children with dyslexia (including recent works using lexical surprisal: Klimovich-Gray et al., 2023; Salig et al., preprint), we did not anticipate finding group differences at lexico-semantic levels of processing, but expected that children with dyslexia may be less effective at tracking phonological, and possibly syntactic, surprisal at the neural level.

text.text: Together, these two studies are aiming to inform both theory and methodological approaches to understanding language development and processing, and how these may vary in relation to reading ability and dyslexia-related variations between learners.
Study 1 observed data from 140 typically developing English monolingual children ages 7 to 12 years (M = 9.06, SD = 1.21), ranging from Grades 1 to 5.
The sample included 56.4% of children who identified as female, 42.9% as male, and one child (.7%) as nonbinary.
All participants were from the United States Midwest, with 72.1% being white, 4.3% Asian, 4.3% Black or African American and 19.3% reporting multiple races.
Caregiver education level was collected through questionnaires and served as a proxy for socioeconomic status.
Mean education level was 6.28 (SD = 0.99; range = 0 to 8), indicating having completed a bachelor's degree.

All children attained standard scores of 86 or higher on standardized measures of phonological awareness and word reading, did not have a history of epilepsy, seizures, traumatic brain injury, or other severe neurological conditions, and did not have a formal diagnosis of dyslexia.

As the recruitment process was geared toward children with reading difficulties, some parents of children in the Study 1 sample did report language-related concerns, but all included children met the standard score thresholds and were therefore treated as typically developing.

To examine potential differences during listening in children with dyslexia, 35 children (31.4% female, 68.6% male) were identified from a larger dataset based on a number of key factors commonly associated with dyslexia.
This subset of children had an average age of 9.34 years (SD = 1.15) across Grades 1 through 5.
The ethnicity breakdown of the sample is as follows: 74.2% White, 2.9% Latino, 2.9% Black, 2.9% Middle Eastern or North African, and 17.1% reported multiple races.
The mean caregiver education level was 6 (SD = 1.07), corresponding to having attained a bachelor's degree.
At the time of data collection, dyslexia screening was not required in public schools in the region of data collection, so many children with reading difficulties had no formal diagnosis.
We therefore included children both with and without a prior diagnosis, and used a stricter cutoff for those without a formal diagnosis.

Children with a formal diagnosis were included if they scored at least 1 SD below the normed mean (standard score ≤ 85; M = 100, SD = 15) on at least two of four measures: the Elision subtest of the Comprehensive Test of Phonological Processing (CTOPP-2; Wagner et al., 2013), the Sight Word Efficiency and Phonemic Decoding Efficiency subtests of the Test of Word Reading Efficiency (TOWRE-2; Torgesen et al., 2012), and the Letter-Word Identification subtest of the Woodcock-Johnson IV Tests of Achievement (Schrank et al., 2014).

Once the dyslexia sample had been identified, 35 children (31.4% female, 68.6% male) from the typically developing sample in Study 1 were age-and gender-matched for group comparison purposes.

Similar to the other samples in this study, the mean caregiver education level was 6.50 (SD = 0.87).
Participants were invited to an in-person laboratory visit that lasted approximately 3 hours.

Caregivers and children were first asked for informed consent and assent, followed by caregivers being asked to fill out survey questionnaires about their children's learning experiences, medical history, and demographic information.
Children were invited to first complete fNIRS testing, followed by behavioral testing.
After testing was completed, participants received monetary compensation.
All consent forms, questionnaires, and testing protocols were IRB approved for human subject testing.
All testing was administered by trained research assistants.
Research assistants were undergraduate and graduate students studying psychology.

text.text: All participants completed the story-listening task under fNIRS neuroimaging.
The task entailed listening to a lab modified, 14-minute-and-54-second version of the Henry Huggins story (Cleary, 2009).

text.text: The story was about a boy named Henry and his new dog.
There were five pauses embedded into the story, at which point children were presented a basic comprehension question with two response options.
An example of a question is "What should Henry do to bring the dog onto the bus?"
with the options "He should get a box" or "He should get a collar".
The child would then have to select their response using a two-button keypad.
After the response, prerecorded feedback was provided, and the story resumed.
Participants first completed a practice round consisting of the first 56 seconds of the story, followed by the task's first question-and-answer segment.
This test portion had 1,956 words and ran 13 minutes and 58 seconds and was used in all analyses for the present study.
Beginning and end times for each word in the presented story were estimated using Praat software (Boersma et al., 2026) and the Montreal Forced Aligner (McAuliffe et al., 2017).

text.text: Surprisal values for the next word, the initial phoneme of the next word, and the word's part-ofspeech were calculated for each word of the audio stimulus as described in the next section.

Lexical surprisal reflects the overall contextual predictability of a given word based on preceding discourse context, quantifying how unexpected a specific lexical item is within the ongoing narrative.

As previously mentioned, lexical surprisal estimates have been shown to have a reliable relation to N400 responses (Michaelov et al., 2024), electrophysiological reactions which are traditionally thought to capture dissonance in meaning-related processing (Kutas & Federmeier, 2000; Kutas & Hillyard, 1980).

text.text: Initial phoneme surprisal, from this point on referred to as phonological surprisal, indexes the bottom-up phonological predictability of a word's starting speech sound given the preceding phonetic context, capturing early auditory expectations prior to full lexical access and retrieval.

Part-of-speech surprisal, or syntactic surprisal, captures the syntactic expectancy of a word's grammatical category; for instance, whether a noun, verb, or adjective was most expected given the prior context window.
This measure was employed to reflect how well each word fits into the expected structural framework of a coherent narrative passage.
Surprisal estimation.
Our protocol for the estimation of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal followed the approach of Heilbron et al. (2022), adapted for use with fNIRS data.

text.text: We used GPT-2 small to estimate surprisal via the Hugging Face Transformers package in Python, the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary (Carnegie Mellon University, 2014) through the Natural Language Toolkit library (Bird et al., 2009) for the initial phoneme estimations, and spaCy (Honnibal et al., 2020) for part-of-speech tagging for the syntactic surprisal values.

text.text: Lexical surprisal was calculated as the negative log-probability assigned to each word by GPT-2, given its prior context (Hale, 2001; Levy, 2008).

text.text: Part-of-speech (e.g., syntactic) surprisal was calculated by, first, sampling k next word tokens given the left-context where k was set to the greater of 50 or the number of tokens whose probability summed to 0.9.
Next, we summed the model's predicted probabilities across the next-word candidates that shared the same part-ofspeech tag as the target word.
The negative log of that summed probability was used for modeling.

Phonological surprisal followed a similar calculation: the initial phoneme of each word was identified, all predicted probabilities of the k next-word candidates sharing that same initial phoneme were summed, and then the negative log of the summed probability was used for modeling.

All models also accounted for word rate (a baseline control for the auditory features of each word) and lexical frequency, which was compiled from a database of HAL frequency counts (Balota et al., 2007).

text.text: Preprocessing of fNIRS data.
Preparation and preprocessing of fNIRS hemodynamic response data was conducted in MATLAB using the AnalyzIR Toolbox for fNIRS (Santosa et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Preparation and preprocessing of fNIRS hemodynamic response data was conducted in MATLAB using the AnalyzIR Toolbox for fNIRS <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Santosa et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Preprocessing steps included optical density conversion, temporal derivative distribution repair (TDDR) motion correction, applying the modified Beer-Lambert law, downsampling the data to 4Hz, and trimming data to remove question-answer sections, thus leaving only story listening portions for analysis.
Subject and group-level modeling.
Hemodynamic responses were modeled using a twolevel general linear model (GLM) in the AnalyzIR Toolbox.

At the subject level, HbO amplitude in each of 32 channels was modeled as a function of five regressors, each convolved with the canonical hemodynamic response function (peak at 6 seconds): word rate (1 at each word onset, controlling for acoustic onsets), log word frequency, and lexical, phonological, and syntactic surprisal.

Short-separation channels were included as nuisance regressors to correct for systemic physiological noise, and estimation used autoregressive iteratively reweighted least squares (AR-IRLS; Barker et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Short-separation channels were included as nuisance regressors to correct for systemic physiological noise, and estimation used autoregressive iteratively reweighted least squares (AR-IRLS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Barker et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: At the group level, beta coefficients were modeled with mixed-effects models including condition, age as a covariate, and a random intercept for each subject.
Results were plotted at p < .05, and channels surviving false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q < .05) are marked with asterisks in Figures 1 and 2.

text.text: For Study One's moderator analysis, the same first-level analysis procedure was used, but the second level included interaction terms created between each condition and WJ-IV Passage Comprehension (PC) raw scores (used as a proxy for reading proficiency).

Age was included as a covariate in the reading proficiency model, to examine the effect of reading proficiency above and beyond natural maturation with age, as well as real word reading scores (TOWRE SWE) to account for baseline decoding ability.
This approach was also employed to examine the role of reading proficiency within the dyslexia sample using the same model parameters.

For Study Two's group comparison, the second-level model included a categorical group variable, coded as TD (typically developing) or DYS (dyslexia), to examine whether neural tracking of each condition differed by reading-difficulty status.
Group category was entered as an interaction term with condition rather than as a main effect, and age was included as a covariate.
In this model, each condition's association with hemodynamic response was estimated separately for the TD and DYS groups.

Group differences for each condition were tested using planned contrasts on the group-by-condition interaction terms, comparing the beta coefficient for the dyslexia (DYS) group against the typically developing (TD) group within each surprisal condition separately (e.g., DYS -TD for lexical surprisal).
As mentioned, in order to account for acoustic and lexical influences, all analyses included word rate and log word frequency as control predictors.
Rate, which captures acoustic onsets, was positively linked to activation across bilateral superior temporal, temporoparietal, and parietal regions.
Only one observation in the right hemisphere parietal lobe did not survive FDR correction.

For this analysis, we observed two participant samples: a sample of 35 children with dyslexia, both with and without formal diagnoses, and a subsample of typically developing sample age-and gender-matched to the identified children with dyslexia.

The age and gender matched TD sample (n = 35) showed a pattern broadly similar to that of the full TD sample: negative frontal tracking in a frontal channel for phonological surprisal, positive temporal tracking for lexical surprisal, and substantial right hemisphere tracking of syntactic surprisal.
Due to finding overall similar patterns, despite much lower power for the subsample of matched TD children, we will focus on results from children with dyslexia from this point on.

text.text: Contrasts between the dyslexia and matched TD groups yielded findings at exploratory thresholds and therefore should be treated as potential trends.
For phonological surprisal, the matched TD group demonstrated greater tracking than the dyslexia group in the left parietal region, specifically a channel near the supramarginal gyrus.

In contrast, the dyslexia group demonstrated greater lexical surprisal tracking in the bilateral posterior STG than the matched TD group, as well as greater tracking for syntactic surprisal in the left anterior STG.
The matched TD group demonstrated greater syntactic surprisal tracking in right temporoparietal and posterior STG regions.
A central question in dyslexia research is how the phonological weaknesses often observed in this population relate to other language systems.
Using naturalistic story listening, we asked how neural tracking of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal relates to reading proficiency in children with and without dyslexia.
Syntactic surprisal tracking was positively related to reading proficiency in both groups, whereas relations for phonological and lexical tracking appeared to diverge at exploratory thresholds.
Among typically developing children, better readers showed stronger phonological tracking.
Among children with dyslexia, better readers showed weaker phonological tracking but stronger lexical tracking, a pattern generally mirrored by direct group contrasts.
These findings are consistent with accounts in which language subsystems develop interdependently (e.g., Werker, 2018; Wolf et al., 2024).

text.text: We discuss each linguistic level in turn and then consider the theoretical implications.

The present findings suggest that the developing brain is likely making predictions at multiple levels, as has been documented previously in adults (e.g., Heilbron et al., 2022; Ryskin & Niewland, 2023), but that recruitment may shift with maturity and reading skill.

text.text: In contrast, we found more widespread activation for phonological tracking of surprisal in children with dyslexia, likely reflecting a lack of specialization for this group.

When compared to an age-and gender-matched control group, the control group showed more activation in the supramarginal gyrus, a region key for phonological processing and literacy development (e.g., Booth et al., 2004; Sliwinska et al., 2012), over the dyslexia group, at an exploratory threshold.

text.text: Additionally, while we found an FDR-corrected positive relationship between frontal tracking of phonological surprisal and reading proficiency in our typically developing sample, we found negative correlations in frontal and parietal regions for children with dyslexia at exploratory thresholds, suggesting that as reading proficiency increases, tracking of phonological surprisal may decrease as these children find different strategies and pathways to reading.
The trends of these findings fit our hypothesis that children with dyslexia may show reduced tracking of phonological surprisal relative to their TD counterparts.

This hypothesis was informed by decades of research (see Snowling & Melby-Lervåg, 2016 for a meta-analysis) showing that phonological difficulties are a core contributor to differences in the linguistic processing of children with dyslexia, and the present study contributes that this may continue to be the case even during a naturalistic listening task not specifically designed to isolate phonological awareness.

text.text: However, the relationship between lexical surprisal tracking and reading proficiency showed opposite trends between groups.

Among children with dyslexia, stronger tracking in the left superior temporal gyrus (STG) was associated with better reading proficiency, a robust effect that survived FDRcorrection and showed greater tracking than in typically developing children at an exploratory threshold in the group comparison.
Typically developing children, by contrast, showed only negative relations to reading comprehension at exploratory thresholds.
One possible interpretation is that the lexical surprisal effects reflect, in part, children's use of higher-level meaning to anticipate upcoming words.

Taken together, these results suggest that syntactic surprisal tracking, as measured by part-of-speech categorization, in children with dyslexia largely parallels that of typically developing children.

One explanation for this unexpected pattern is that prior work on syntax in dyslexia has largely focused on morphosyntax, such as inflectional morphology and subject-verb agreement (e.g., Rispens & Been, 2004), whose fine-grained features are closely tied to phonological processing (Casani et al., 2022).

text.text: By examining neural tracking at all three levels simultaneously, the present study revealed a pattern that isolated measures might miss: weaker phonological tracking in children with dyslexia co-occurred with robust lexical and syntactic tracking, both of which were positively related to passage comprehension.
The relation between syntactic tracking and reading proficiency was shared across groups, suggesting that categorylevel syntactic processing may remain largely intact in dyslexia.
This is consistent with metaanalytic evidence that structural syntactic skills contribute to reading comprehension from early elementary into secondary school (Tong et al., 2025).

text.text: Based on the promising findings of the present study at largely exploratory thresholds, further validating and refining the present study's multi-level surprisal approach may lead to useful implications for clinical and educational practice, such as informing intervention design and assessment features that work to identify the strengths children with dyslexia can leverage for improved reading outcomes.
Several limitations in this work come from the novelty of this experimental design.
First, phonological surprisal was indexed only at the word-initial phoneme level.
This measure was chosen due to its ability to adapt to the slow hemodynamic response measured by fNIRS, as this method of neuroimaging is unlikely to be able to resolve phoneme-by-phoneme timing.
Second, all surprisal values were derived from GPT-2, a large language model (LLM) trained predominantly on adult-authored and adult-directed text.

Due to these developmental differences, it remains unclear how well these estimates capture what a child listener might find predictable or surprising at each linguistic level compared to adult expectations.
These limitations point to several directions for future work.
Methods with finer temporal resolution, such as EEG or MEG, could examine a wider range of LLM-derived measures in children.

Additionally, Study 2 intentionally included both children with formal dyslexia diagnoses and children identified as at risk using standardized assessment thresholds, focusing on children actively experiencing reading difficulties.

Future work may extend this approach to children with dyslexia who have received substantial remediation and, thus, show higher performance in reading to examine whether patterns of neural tracking shift with intervention.

The two studies presented in the current manuscript demonstrate that linguistic surprisal, estimated using LLMs at the phonological, lexical, and syntactic levels, meaningfully tracks children's hemodynamic responses during a naturalistic listening task.
This novel approach offers a viable alternative to explicit, trial-based methodological paradigms that have traditionally been used to study childhood neurolinguistic development.

The results of Study 1 show largely converging evidence with prior developmental literature for typically developing children, while Study 2 offered a promising extension of this approach to children at-risk for or diagnosed with dyslexia.
The latter examination revealed subtle differences in the balance of tracking across different linguistic levels for the dyslexia group.

The present findings extend traditional psycholinguistic and clinical approaches to measuring language processing and highlight potential areas of strength for children with dyslexia, offering potential avenues for future intervention and clinical work aimed at teaching compensatory strategies for improving literacy development.
